catalog_locator: Appendix A 'Summary of the phonemic analysis as it relates to the orthography used', §3 'Tone', items b-c, p. 293; Appendix B 'Punctuation', p. 294. (archive.org; same pages also in the ERIC ED046003 scan text, page markers '- 293 -', '- 294 -').
catalog_quote: Phonetically we have also to distinguish between high and low pitch. This is however conditioned by the vowel quality as follows: Breathy vowels always have low pitch, and clear vowels in the corresponding position always have high pitch. But within each of these two categories we have a phonemic contrast between level pitch and contour pitch. These features, however, are not a characteristic of the syllable, but of the morpheme. In morphemes with initial breathy syllables we have low level pitch contrasting with a low-rising-falling contour. ... In morphemes with initial clear syllables we have high level pitch contrasting with an extra-high-falling contour. ... c. Affixes. Breathy affixes are tonic, that is, they manifest a constant low pitch throughout their distribution. For the clear affixes, there are two categories: tonic and atonic. ... The clear level affixes are atonic. Their pitch is conditioned by the nature of the stem to which they are affixed ... [p. 293] ... The last syllable starts with a heavy intonational stress. The intensity fades away very quickly and at the same time the pitch also drops quickly. (Intonational stress is realized as a pitch upstep and general intensity on the stressed syllable.) ... It signals a heavy intonational stress on the first syllable of the question word (upstep in pitch and intensity) and a less heavier stress on the question morpheme. [p. 294]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Thakali (thak1245) is not in the catalog. The single title hit, Pittman 1970 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies' (Part II of the 1970 Tone Systems report, full djvu text already held by the project), was read in full: it is a comparative register/tone paper giving Thakali word-bases four pitch/voice-quality classes (clear high level, clear extra-high falling, breathy low rising-falling, breathy low level) and says nothing about word-stress placement in Thakali (its 'stressed/unstressed' labels are Tamang). Beyond the title hit: Hari & Maibaum 1970 Appendix A/B (held by the project, read) describe a morpheme-level tone/register system and only utterance-level intonational stress; Sharma 2008 'Thakali language: A phonemic overview' (Nepalese Linguistics 23, downloaded today, text) has no stress statement and defers to Hari 1970 for tone; Sharma 2006 (held by the project, scanned) is silent. Not obtainable: Hari 1970 'Thakali tone and higher levels' (Part I, ERIC ED046001 'PDF pending restoration', not on archive.org; HathiTrust/Google Books blocked) — the highest-priority acquisition, since the ERIC abstract says Part I analyses 'stress group' and foot-nucleus units; Georg 1996 Marphatan Thakali and Regmi et al. 2010 A grammar of Thakali are print-only (medium priority).org, ERIC, Digital Himalaya's Nepalese Linguistics ToC and Glottolog.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Thakali is described as a pitch/tone language: each morpheme carries one of four prosodies (clear high level, clear extra-high falling, breathy low level, breathy low rising-falling), pitch register being conditioned by breathy vs clear vowels and the level-vs-contour contrast being phonemic at the morpheme level; clear level affixes are atonic and take their pitch from the stem. Stress is treated only as an intonational (utterance-level) feature realized as pitch upstep plus intensity, e.g. a heavy stress on the last syllable of the utterance under certain intonation patterns and on the first syllable of a question word; no word-level stress position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords add voiced stops and a nasalized vowel; irregularities in tone are not discussed in the opened pages.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is stated to be a property of the morpheme (word-base), with tonic/atonic affixes; 'stress' in the source is intonational and belongs to the utterance (phrase) level, described through punctuation symbols used in the texts. Preliminary SIL field analysis (1969-70), presented as a summary appended to a text collection rather than a full phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Hari & Maibaum 1970) is SIL work on the Thakali of the Thak Khola (texts include the Tulachan clan legend and a trip to the Thak Khola; Sharma 2006 divides Thakali into Tukuche, Marphatan and Syang dialects, differing in 'tone and pitch'); the opened pages do not name the dialect explicitly. Georg 1996 describes the Marpha village variety ('Marphatan Thakali', listed by Glottolog as an alternative name under thak1245, no separate glottocode). All are treated under thak1245.

new_statements.reading: The only first-hand prosodic description of Thakali readable in this search of works with stress in the title. It describes word prosody as a morpheme-level tone/register system (clear vs breathy, level vs contour pitch; clear level affixes atonic, taking the stem's pitch) and describes 'stress' only as an utterance-level intonational feature (pitch upstep + intensity), placed by intonation pattern, typically on the last syllable of the utterance. It states no lexical word-stress rule, so for a stress catalog Thakali should be coded from this as a tone/register language with no reported word stress (silent on fixed placement), pending Hari 1970 Part I.

tone_statements.quote: The preceding examples induce us to set up a four box contrast system. We have already seen that tense voice quality conditions high pitch and laxness low pitch. Within each group we have a further contrast between level and contour pitches. The two intersecting systems of tense versus lax voice quality and level versus gliding pitch result in a four way contrast. [table] GLIDING | LEVEL; TENSE (relatively high): extra high falling I ('v) | high, basically level II (v); LAX (relatively low): low rising falling III ('vh) | low, basically level IV (vh)
tone_statements.locator: p. 37, section I.2 'Pitch contrast', subsection 'The Four Box Contrast System' (prose + four-box table)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive pitch patterns per morpheme: tense (high) vs lax (low) voice quality crossed with level vs gliding pitch; stem contour spreads over neutral suffixes; word stress on first syllable.

sources.note: Pitch is conditioned by vowel register (breathy = low, clear = high) with a phonemic level-vs-contour contrast that is a property of the morpheme, not the syllable; affixes are tonic or atonic. Stress is mentioned only as 'intonational stress' (pitch upstep + intensity) placed by utterance-level intonation patterns (e.g. heavy stress on the last syllable of the utterance before ') ' or '!', on the first syllable of a question word); no word-stress placement rule is given.

sources.citation: Sharma (Gautam), Narayan P. (2008). Thakali language: A phonemic overview. Nepalese Linguistics 23: 355-370 (Digital Himalaya ToC prints 343-354).
sources.quote: It is basically a monosyllabic language. Most of the morphemes are formed of a single syllable. ... The study of tone on Thakali has been made in detail by Hari (1970). The Thakali tone system may be characterized in terms of two kinds of contrasts - contrasts for breathiness and contrast for pitch contour. The contrast between breathy and clear is relevant only to the onset of a morpheme while the pitch contour of a morpheme extends over the whole morpheme (Hari, 1970).
sources.locator: §6 Syllables and Syllabification, §7 Tone, pp. 367-369 (txt lines ~12189-12250)
sources.note: No mention of stress anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent the whole volume text: 'stress' occurs only in unrelated articles). Word prosody described as tone (breathiness + pitch contour), following Hari 1970. Also read Sharma 2006 (NL 22, scanned held by the project): silent on stress.

Lehman (ed.), Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal, Part II: Lexical lists and comparative studies (Occasional Papers of the Wolfenden Society on Tibeto-Burman Linguistics III), pp. 1-8. Urbana: University of Illinois.
sources.quote: In the early fall of 1969, Maria Hari ... described Thakali word-bases as being either (a) clear high level, (b) clear extra-high falling, (c) breathy low rising-falling, or (d) breathy low level. ... words which are (a) high stressed in Tamang are clear intense in Gurung and clear high level in Thakali, (b) unstressed in Tamang are clear relaxed in Gurung and clear extra-high falling in Thakali, (c) mid stressed in Tamang are breathy rising in Gurung and breathy low rising-falling in Thakali, and (d) low stressed in Tamang are breathy low in Gurung and breathy low level in Thakali
sources.locator: Pittman chapter = djvu-text lines ~351-850 (printed pp. 1-8), esp. sections 2-3 and Table 3
sources.note: Reports Hari's (fall 1969) analysis: 'Thakali word-bases may be (a) clear high level, (b) clear extra-high falling, (c) breathy low rising-falling, or (d) breathy low level'; contrasts this with Tamang, whose four classes are defined by stress (high/mid/low stressed vs unstressed); states that 'Stress, relative pitch, pitch contour, intensity and breathiness carry a high proportion of the functional load of the register system in T[amang], Gu[rung], and Th[akali]'. No word-stress position for Thakali.
sources.venue: Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal 2: Lexical lists and comparative studies

tone.quote: Hari (1970: 125-142) has identified two kinds of contrasts in tone in Thakali: contrast for breathiness (tense vs. lax)) and contrasts for pitch contour. Thus, assuming Thakali as a tonal language, the canonical structure of the syllable at the maximum may be presented as in (26).8 (26) (T) (Ci) (X) V (Cf) ... 8 At present, tone, a suprasegmental property, may be debatable in Thakali. tone.quote: In Tamang (Mazaudon 1973b:61-92) ... Each such word, whatever the number of its syllables and the number of its compounding morphemes, has one of four possible melodies. There are no stress differences among the syllables, no unstressed or weak syllables and no syllables with a neutral vowel. The phonological word as the domain of tonal oppositions is a feature common to most of the tonal languages of the Bodic division in Nepal as yet studied (Hale and Pike 1970 passim; Pike 1970:153).

tone.quote: The preceding examples induce us to set up a four box contrast system. We have already seen that tense voice quality conditions high pitch and laxness low pitch. Within each group we have a further contrast between level and contour pitches. The two intersecting systems of tense versus lax voice quality and level versus gliding pitch result in a four way contrast. [table] GLIDING | LEVEL; TENSE (relatively high): extra high falling I ('v) | high, basically level II (v); LAX (relatively low): low rising falling III ('vh) | low, basically level IV (vh)
